subject: TTFT & streaming probe — post-demo clarifications and pilot plan

From: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.ai>

Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>

Subject: TTFT & streaming probe — post-demo clarifications and pilot plan

Alex — thanks again for the demo time today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we keep momentum: 

Summary of Veridian's targets (as discussed):
- TTFT median target: ~200ms for typical instruction prompts (~512 tokens pre-context)
- 95th percentile target: <450ms
- Sustained throughput target: ~400 RPS during peak window (burst to ~800 for 30s)
- Concurrent streams: up to 120 concurrent websocket/SSE clients
- Streaming behavior: prefer WebSocket for latency-sensitive clients, SSE fallback for browsers where WS is not available
- Chunk cadence preference: small chunks (50–150ms cadence) for progressive UI updates

What Redwood will do next:
1) Share a minimal probe script and a short runbook (attached) you can run against our hosted test endpoint. It includes both WebSocket and SSE probes plus a quick cURL example.
2) Karthik will follow up on engineering specifics (chunk framing, priming/primed cache behavior, recommended concurrency tuning).
3) We propose a 2-week pilot: baseline measurements (hosted), then a dedicated pilot run on reserved capacity if the baseline shows gaps.

Immediate asks for you:
- Confirm the traffic profile we should emulate (attach if you already have it).
- Confirm timezones for a 30–45 minute engineer call (we're suggesting Mon/Tue next week).

Attachments: redwood-ttft-mini-plan.pdf (short plan), ttft_probe_script.sh (probe script).

Thanks — i'll loop Karthik for technical follow-up.

— Vivek Kulkarni
Director, Solutions Engineering
Redwood Inference

From: Alex Gomez <alex.gomez@veridian.ai>

Cc: eng-team@veridian.ai
Date: Wed, 28 Jul 2027 16:20:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: TTFT & streaming probe — post-demo clarifications and pilot plan

Thanks Vivek — useful recap. A couple quick clarifications from our side before we run the probe: 

1) WebSocket vs SSE: we prefer WS for our desktop product but will keep SSE for web fallback. Are there differences we should expect in TTFT between WS and SSE on Redwood's hosted path?

2) Chunking behavior: when you say 50–150ms cadence, is that per-chunk or per-token? We typically render per-chunk; our UI tolerates 80–100ms cadence nicely.

3) Cold starts / KV cache: our workload has many short lived sessions (10–20 tokens of user prompt + 256 token model), how do you recommend priming? Can Redwood do a warmstart profile or keep active KV caches across short sessions?

I've attached our high-level traffic profile (veridian-traffic-profile.csv). For the initial run please emulate a 10-minute window at the peak RPS.

Finally, could you include a tiny example (curl/ws) we can drop into our perf lab? If you can schedule the engineer call Tues (UTC-7) morning that works for our team.

— Alex
Head of Platform
Veridian AI

[Attachment: veridian-traffic-profile.csv (CSV)]

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Gomez <alex.gomez@veridian.ai>
Cc: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 29 Jul 2027 09:10:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: TTFT & streaming probe — post-demo clarifications and pilot plan

Alex — Karthik here (engineer on inference runtime). Answering your bullets and adding concrete examples you can try in your perf lab.

On WS vs SSE:
- There is no inherent extra processing cost difference in our runtime between WS and SSE; the main difference is client-side framing and network stack behavior. WebSocket tends to have slightly lower jitter on browsers and is our recommendation for latency-sensitive desktop clients. Expect < ~20ms difference in practice (client+browser dependent).

Chunking cadence notes:
- Our chunking is framing-based (we group tokens into chunks before flushing). When I say 50–150ms cadence that is the inter-chunk interval we target during steady emission, not per-token. Typical chunk sizes for your latency target: 8–16 tokens per chunk at 8k model throughput, which yields the cadence band you mentioned.

Cold starts & KV cache warmstart:
- For short sessions we recommend a priming warmstart step: send a small warm request that populates the KV cache before the real user request (we can do this as part of the probe).
- On dedicated capacity we can keep KV cache resident for warm pools; hosted runs will be best-effort but we can configure sticky routing for the pilot to increase cache hits.

Suggested minimal examples (included inline for quick copy):
- cURL (SSE fallback):
  curl -s -N -H "Authorization: Bearer <TEST_KEY>" 
    https://api.redwood.ai/v1/streams?model=redwood-8k 
    -d '{"input":"<prompt>","stream":true}'

- quick JS WebSocket snippet (pseudo):
  const ws = new WebSocket('wss://ws.api.redwood.ai/v1/stream?model=redwood-8k');
  ws.onopen = () => ws.send(JSON.stringify({key: '<TEST_KEY>', input: '<prompt>', stream: true}));
  ws.onmessage = (m) => console.log('chunk', m.data);

Pilot tuning suggestions:
- Start pilot with 50 concurrent clients ramping to 120 over 5 minutes; run three 10-minute peak windows across an hour to mimic burstiness.
- Use a priming token (3–5 token warm call) 30s before each client session for best 95th percentile.
- Observe both TTFT and first-chunk size; if TTFT is fine but UI stutters, increase chunk size slightly.

Attaching the small probe script and a snippet doc for SSE/WS examples. I'll be on the Tuesday engineer call to help interpret traces.

— Karthik Iyer
Principal Software Engineer, Serving Runtime
Redwood Inference

[Attachment: ttft_probe_script.sh (bash script)]
[Attachment: sse-ws-sample-snippets.md (text)]
